chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from his father, from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad Al-Jawhari, from Jamil ibn Salih, from Abd al-Malik ibn Amr Al-Ahwal, who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) recited this verse: 'And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are moderate between those [extremes]'.
He said: So he took a handful of pebbles and closed his hand tightly around them, then said: 'This is the stinginess (al-iqtar) which Allah mentioned in His book'.
Then he took another handful, so he opened his palm completely, then said: 'This is the extravagance (al-israf)'.
Then he took another handful, so he opened part of it and withheld part of it, and said: 'This is the moderation (al-qawam)'.

key_terms.إِسْرَافٌ: Extravagance or spending excessively beyond need.
key_terms.قَبْضَةً: A handful (used here as a physical metaphor for holding wealth).
key_terms.قَوَامٌ: Moderation or a firm, balanced standing between two extremes.

ai.seo_question: How did the Imam explain the meaning of 'moderation' in spending according to Surah Al-Furqan?
ai.summary: In this renowned hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) provides a tangible pedagogical demonstration of the Quranic virtue of *Qasr* (moderation) by physically manipulating pebbles to distinguish between miserliness (*Iqtar*), extravagance (*Israf*), and the balanced middle path (*Qawam*). This narration is foundational in Shia jurisprudence and ethics for defining financial prudence, illustrating that true moderation is not merely the arithmetic mean but a dynamic state of holding back excess while avoiding the deprivation of needs. The physical act underscores the spiritual discipline required to maintain equilibrium in worldly transactions.
